records.abstract: 이 연구는 2008년부터 2021년까지의 시군구 수준 데이터를 이용하여, 청년인구의 고용률이 결혼과 출산에 미친 효과를 추정하였다. 지역의 전체 고용률과 남성 고용률 증가는 무배우 여성의 혼인율과 여성인구 유배우 비율을 높이는 것으로 나타났다. 반면, 여성 고용률 증가는 해당 지역 내 여성의 유배우 비율과 유배우 출산율을 낮춤으로써 합계출산율을 감소시키는 역할을 하였다. 이러한 성별 차이는 여성이 노동시장에서 겪는 결혼과 출산의 패널티로 인해, 고용 여건 개선이 결혼과 출산의 기회비용을 높였기때문에 나타난 것으로 추정된다. 논문의 결과는 여성 고용을 양적으로 확대하는 노력과 함께 일자리에서 여성이 경험하는 결혼과 출산의 불리함을 제거하기 위한 정책적 노력을 강화해야 할 필요성을 확인해 준다.

records.title: The effect of alimony on married women's labor supply and fertility: Evidence from state‐level reforms
records.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
records.abstract: Abstract Reforms that reduce spousal support after divorce are generally thought to reduce the bargaining power of alimony recipients as well as their incentives to participate in the traditional model of household specialization. Using the U.S. Time Use Survey and exploiting a series of recent reforms in several U.S. states that reduced the rights of eligible spouses, we find that wives surprised by the reforms reacted by increasing their labor supply, but the adjustment mechanism varied by educational group. While college educated wives' labor supply increased at the expense of time spent on housework and childcare, wives with less than a college degree sacrificed personal care and leisure time. Effects for men are generally smaller and not statistically significant. We also find a reduction in the rate of new births following the reforms, with the effect being much more pronounced in the case of women with a university education, suggesting that part of the difference in time use may be attributable to differences in preferences and the cost of children by educational levels. Since children are a marital public good, our results imply a decrease in marriage‐specific investment. The estimated effects are robust to various sensitivity tests and are greater in couples with a high‐income differential and therefore more exposed to changes in alimony laws.

records.title: A cost analysis comparing Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention with and without Vitamin A Supplementation among under-5 children in Nigeria
records.abstract: Abstract Background Child mortality in Nigeria, significantly affected by malaria and malnutrition, remains a public health concern in the country. Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC) and Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) are effective interventions that can be delivered through integrated health campaigns to reduce this mortality. This study assesses the cost implications of integrating these two interventions among under-5 children in Northeast Nigeria. Methods A cost analysis compared standalone SMC (Cycle 1 in July 2021) with SMC-VAS integrated campaign (Cycle 4 in October 2023) in two Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Bauchi State. The number of children reached by the SMC-only campaign was 168,820 and for the SMC+Vit A campaign, the number was 170,681. Data collection utilized a mixed-methods approach, drawing from primary and secondary sources, including programmatic, financial, and coverage records. Costs were categorized into distribution, Sulphadoxine-Pyrimethamine plus Amodaiquine (SPAQ) for SMC, Vitamin A, training, supplies, meetings, labor, supervision, and social mobilization costs. Sensitivity analyses evaluated the effect of a 10% fluctuation in the costs of distribution, labor, SPAQ, and supplies on the cost per child. Results The total cost for the SMC standalone campaign was US$158,934, and the SMC-VAS integration was US$186,426. Distribution and drug costs were the largest contributors in the integrated and SMC-only campaign. The SMC-only cost per child was $0.94 and $1.18 when eligible children received both SMC and VAS. The integration of VAS into the SMC campaign cycle incurred an additional US$27,492 over Cycle 1 cost (US$186,426 - US$158,934). Fluctuations in distribution costs were the most influential component of the cost per child. Conclusion Integrating VAS with SMC campaigns increases the cost by US$0.24 per child, a modest increment considering the potential health benefits. The results support the feasibility of this integration, in terms of cost, to combat child mortality from malaria and malnutrition in Nigeria. Further research is recommended to explore the cost-effectiveness of this integrated distribution model.

records.title: The unbearable (financial) burdens of parenting
records.abstract: Taking Nigel Dodd's work on the social life of money as a springboard (Dodd (2014) 2016), Nina Bandelj makes an impassioned call to extend his approach to studying the social life of money spent on children. In the process she draws attention to the transformation that has taken place in the last few decades in the United States to increasingly view children as sites of parental financial investment. Radically increased spending, saving and borrowing for children is part of relational work, in which today's parents are expected to engage so that they can help their children develop the necessary skills to thrive later in life. A large portion of these parental expenses are educational expenses, like tuition for higher and sometimes secondary education, a wide swath of enrichment activities (like sports and theater camps), and supplementary education offerings like math tutoring and SAT preparatory classes. In her analysis of parental expenses on children, Bandelj also includes expensive mortgages that buy families access to high-performing public school districts. This is because public school education in the United States is mainly financed through local property taxes, and the price of real estate in towns with high-performing schools reflects this. In making her argument, Bandelj echoes Viviana Zelizer's work on the historical and cultural transformation that took place in the United States at the end of the 19th—early 20th century when children went from being perceived as economically useful to being viewed as economically valueless but emotionally priceless (Zelizer, 1985). Recently, Bandelj contends, children are increasingly being treated as sites of parental investment into their human capital. To be sure, Bandelj acknowledges that “the emotional pricelessness of children is still quite salient” (Bandelj, page xx), yet she argues that the “human capital child” is now taking center stage as mere “childrearing expenditures” that characterized parental spending on children in much of the 20th century are replaced with much more ambitious and future-oriented “parental investments”. This means that the social value of children is being transformed yet again. It now encompasses skill-building that can start very early on, as early as in utero, in order to increase children's future productivity and help them command a better price in a future labor market. Moreover, this cultural shift does not only re-evaluate what childrearing should look like today, and what ends it should pursue, but it also puts the spotlight on parental identities and what it means to be a good parent. Citing both qualitative and quantitative data, Bandelj calls for a comprehensive approach to studying how money flows in households, particularly in relations between parents and children. Such a comprehensive approach would not only account for the cultural changes like the widely-shared emphasis on intensive parenting, or the belief in the utmost importance of higher education for children's future life chances. It would also highlight the structural changes that both necessitate greater parental investments, such as growing educational costs, and the simultaneous reduction in public expenditures on education, and facilitate them. To illustrate the latter point, Bandelj presents evidence on the proliferation of various financial tools like the 529 education savings accounts that allow parents targeted and, sometimes, tax-free savings to pay for children's educational expenses, as well as the parental advice industry instructing on the “proper” and “expected” relations between parents and children, including cultural expectations of parental financial obligations toward their children. Finally, Bandelj concedes that the opportunity to invest in children greatly varies by income and race/ethnicity, and depends on the resources available to parents. A lot of what Nina Bandelj states rings true to me. One cannot deny the steep rise of education costs, and the proliferation of various financial instruments to help parents save and pay for these ever-increasing expenses while they also facilitate their children's competing for admission to highly coveted spots in the nation's top colleges. It is a particularly familiar story to anyone who lives in one of the high-cost towns with excellent public schools, or whose children attend highly competitive high schools, whether public or private. In the rest of this essay, I will raise six points that are intended to nuance this picture, and set scope conditions on some of these claims. In a nutshell, parental investment in children's human capital is indeed a compelling story of what parenting is like financially in the 21st century United States. But it is not the only story to be told. My first point is about clarifying or specifying some of the empirical data used (or drawing attention to the data that are absent). Bandelj provides compelling evidence that parental investments in children are riddled with inequality: families with income in the top decile manage to accumulate significantly more financial assets for their children, and white families accumulate more assets than Black and Hispanic families. At the same time, families in the lower income groups as well as Black families with children are more burdened by educational debt—calculated as share of education debt to all assets—than are higher income families and white families. But why are there no data reported for Asian families? It is particularly unfortunate given that educational attainment and college attendance for Asians surpass those of other racial and ethnic groups, and the extremes of intense (aka “tiger”) parenting are often associated with Asian communities. It would therefore be important to include data on parental investments by Asian parents. Other data may have alternative interpretation. We are told that the much higher debt burden that Black families with children carry (Bandelj, xx, Figure 5) suggests they borrow relatively more to pay for their children's educational expenses. But in a recently published report from the Urban Institute that uses a different data source, we learn that while “blacks are most likely to have student loan debt…we do not find evidence that blacks are more likely than whites or Hispanics to borrow for their child's or grandchild's education” (Braga, 2016, emphasis is mine). Two possible explanations are given: one is that Black families are more credit constrained (Bandelj acknowledges this); the other one is that disproportionally more Blacks enroll in college when they are older. In other words, these student loans are likely for their, and not their children's, education. If this is the case, it is a very significant finding but not the evidence to support the argument about parental investments in children. Finally, some of the empirical evidence presented seems very surprising, and warrants more explanation, for example, the reported average size of the education debt held by families with children: it apparently only grew from $948 in 2001 to $4283 in 2016 (Bandelj, p. xx). These numbers seem very low, and likely include families with zero educational debt. It would be important to know the average (or median) debt held by those families with children that have any debt, and the portion of families with children that belong to this category. Is it possible that we are starting to witness a backlash, if not to the social value of higher education, but to its economic value? It could be a result of higher education costs completely divorcing financial reality of even many upper middle-class families, so that it is not uncommon, for instance, for children to matriculate into more affordable but less prestigious colleges than the most select ones that admitted them (many self-styled college advisors, like Harlan Cohen @harlancohen, advocate for prioritizing affordability and graduating debt-free rather than selectivity/prestige when making the final choice of where to attend). According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, only 22% of surveyed U.S. adults believe that “the cost of college is worth it even if someone has to take loans”, while additional 47% say “worth it, but only without taking out loans,” and 29% say “not worth it” (Fry et al., 2024). Granted, the majority believe it is worth it if one does not have to borrow, and the various financial instruments like 529s do help parents save. However, according to the Education Data Initiative, an average American with a 529 plan has $26,783 saved, which is enough only for one year of attending a public 4-year degree college for one child (Hanson, 2024). As much as parents may feel obligated to invest into their children to assure their futures, middle-age parents also feel obligated to help their own elderly parents, particularly if the latter are incurring high medical or long-term care costs (Zaloom, 2019). And the competing needs must put a considerable damper on parental investments in children. Let's look at the numbers. More than 6 million Americans currently use paid long-term services delivered in home and community settings, and more than 2 million people are residents of institutional settings like nursing homes and assisted living facilities, according to the estimates by the Congressional Budget Office. A likely comparable number of people rely on care provided by unpaid caregivers - family, friends, or neighbors - because they struggle to afford to pay for the services: the estimated average annual cost of nursing home care in the United States is $100,000, and an equivalent cost of assisted living facility or in-home care is $60,000 (Hamel & Montero, 2023). And despite what many Americans may think, Medicare—a federal health insurance for the elderly and some younger people with disabilities—does not pay for the type of long-term care that many elderly Americans will require when they are faced with age-related physical or cognitive decline. It only pays for post-acute skilled nursing care of limited duration, usually up to 100 days. Medicaid—a federal and state program providing health coverage for lower income individuals—does pay for long-term care for those deemed eligible. But to become eligible, families need to go through a process called spend-down, which involves demonstrating that they have limited income and no assets (with some exceptions). Currently, Medicaid pays for about half of overall costs of long-term care in the United States. More than 80% of those over 65 who need long-term care services for five years or more will enroll, including, unexpectedly, half of upper-middle-class couples whose lifetime earnings exceed $4.75 million (Johnson et al., 2021). Are we witnessing another possible backlash to the relentless academic pressures on children to develop skills and earn credentials, and to the financial pressures on parents to invest in building their children's human capital? American families are facing a mental health crisis among American children. Arthur Brooks of The Atlantic reports that according to a recent survey, sponsored by the Walton Family Foundation and fielded by Gallup, 38% of respondents between the ages of 12 to 26 have been formally diagnosed with anxiety or depression, including 29% of men and 45% of women. Additionally, half of those that have not been diagnosed report frequent feelings of anxiety, and a quarter of those undiagnosed report feeling depressed (Brooks, 2004; see also Mehasce, Menasce Horowitz & Graf, 2019). A recent book by Jonathan Haidt calls today's teens and young adults “the anxious generation,” and blames the rise in anxiety on the wide availability of smart phones and social media among children starting from very early age (Haidt, 2024). The COVID pandemic and associated lockdowns and broad disruptions to schooling, recreation and social relations further exacerbated this already growing problem (CDC, undated a). And parents are understandably worried. According to the 2022 Pew Research survey, children's mental health struggles were the number one parental concern with 40% of parents stating that they were extremely/very concerned, and another 36% stating they were somewhat concerned (Gramlich, 2023). Academic pressures are likely not the cause of the crisis of mental illness among teens and young adults, but easing academic pressures is often seen as a solution. Many school districts and college admissions have recently introduced more lenient grading and flexible deadlines or made college admissions test-optional.1 In her book Race at the Top: Asian Americans and Whites in Pursuit of the American Dream in Suburban Schools, Natasha Warikoo (2022) explained that school administrators in a North Eastern town she calls Woodcrest, concerned about the effect of academic pressures and competition on student mental health, implemented policies to reduce the amount of homework that teachers could assign. She also notes that this was a move advocated by white parents who were critical of Asian parents' “tiger parenting” style, and threatened by Asian students' higher academic achievements. The issue of mental health brings me to my fifth point. Both in Viviana Zelizer's original formulation of the social value of children, and in Bandelj's current argument about parental spending, there is one particular blind spot: both only consider the value of healthy children.2 In fact, in the “economically valuable” model of the 19th century discussed in Pricing the Priceless Child, only healthy and able-bodied children had any economic value at all. There are many more children today that live with disabilities or serious illnesses than ever before. According to Pew Research, there are 7.3 million students with disability in the United States, and they comprised 15% of students enrolled in public schools nation-wide in the 2021-22 school year (Schaeffer, 2023). Their parents are faced with a very different set of challenges and expectations (Eichenstein, 2015; Kefalas, 2021). Moreover, in a country like the United States, with its relatively low rate of investments in social services to support families with children, such children usually require a lot of necessary but costly medical and nonmedical therapies that need to be paid for out-of-pocket, and many American parents struggle to do so. In 2012, 36% of families with children reported experiencing financial burden because of medical care costs (Cohen & Kirzinger, 2014). This rate is higher than among families of two or more adults without children (25.2%) or among single adults living on their own (20.1%). To think about the specific costs that parents may incur, let's take Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) as an example. Today, one in every 36 children in the United States in diagnosed with ASD (Autism Speak, undated). The costs of raising a child with ASD may include residential care expenses, special education, various medical and non-medical services (such as diagnostic screening, behavioral, physical and speech therapies, etc.) as well as productivity loss for the parents (Buescher et al., 2014). While in countries with socialized healthcare systems much of these costs are borne by healthcare payers, in the United States, a significant portion of these costs are the responsibility of parents and families. All in all, while the financial burdens on parents of disabled children are often a result of very similar processes documented in public education and reported by Nina Bandelj, such as states shifting responsibility for care away from publicly funded programs to families, these families are likely faced with a set of very different challenges from the world of competitive schooling Bandelj describes. My final point is that it is not only the parental investments in child development and education that we should be closely following, but investment in becoming parents to begin with. The American fertility industry is estimated to be worth $8 billion today. The recent WHO report places the rate of infertility at 17.5% globally (WHO, 2023), but many more people outside these statistics rely on assisted reproductive technologies (ARTs), thanks to changes in cultural attitudes and laws that have made parenting by non-traditional parents, such as same-sex couples, single individuals and older people, much more mainstream. In the United States, the cost of the reliance on ARTs varies from a few hundred dollars for a vial of sperm to more than a hundred thousand dollars for a surrogacy arrangement. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2.3% of babies born in the US are born via IVF (CDC, undated b).3 This number also includes babies born to non-American parents, specifically those that travel to the US in search of surrogacy if it is unavailable or restricted in their country of residence. records.title: Human cognitive enhancement and reprogenetic technologies in Malaysia – A survey study of local Muslim undergraduate students' viewpoints
records.abstract: Introduction: Newly emerging human enhancement technologies such as brain chip implants, CRISPR-Cas9-based gene editing, and polygenic embryo screening (PES) alongside preimplantation genetic testing (PGT-P) are highly controversial in Islam. However, the prevailing sociocultural dynamics encourage their uptake. In the current era of declining fertility rates, increased parental investment in fewer children has resulted in a flourishing tuition industry, accompanied by heightened academic pressure on students and widespread parental anxiety. These emerging technologies can be employed for cognitive enhancement, thereby providing an expedient solution for parents and students navigating a highly competitive educational environment. Materials and methods: To inform and facilitate future policy decision-making, an online survey was conducted among 575 undergraduate Muslim students at the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) to assess their perspectives and opinions regarding these newly emerging technologies. Results: The findings indicated a significant level of opposition among respondents to the uptake of human enhancement technologies, with 54.8% opposing polygenic embryo screening, 69.2% opposing gene editing, and 75.3% opposing brain chip implants, reflecting substantial concerns about altering natural human attributes. The results also indicate that numerous Muslim respondents believe that Allah created humans flawlessly and purposefully, asserting that humanity lacks the authority to alter or amend this creation. Discussion/Conclusion: A three-pronged governance approach for human enhancement technologies is thus proposed, which encompasses (i) bioethical safeguards, (ii) public engagement and education, and (iii) economic accessibility. It is suggested that the Malaysian government should actively consult relevant stakeholders and various segments of the public before enacting future legislation on these technologies.

records.title: Factors Influencing Childbearing Intentions in the Context of Declining Global Fertility Rates: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Introduction Global fertility decline has emerged as a significant demographic challenge, particularly in developing countries, leading to population aging, workforce reduction, and slower economic growth. However, existing evidence lacks a comprehensive synthesis that integrates these multifactorial influences within the global context of fertility decline. This review aims to investigate the multifaceted factors influencing childbearing intentions among couples within the broader context of declining fertility rates, focusing on key individual, demographic, cultural, social, economic, and policy-related factors of reproductive decisions. Methods A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Comprehensive searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2010 and December 2023 that investigated factors associated with childbearing intentions. Fifty studies met the inclusion criteria. Results Findings reveal that individual, demographic, cultural, social, health-related, economic, insurance-related, and governmental factors significantly affect childbearing intentions. Discussion Age, education, and personal attitudes influence fertility intentions, while marital stability and family support strengthen the inclination to have children. Cultural norms shape preferences for larger families, and social support networks further contribute to fertility decisions. Economic stability remains a crucial determinant, as high child costs and financial insecurity often lead to postponing childbearing. Access to healthcare, health insurance, and maternity benefits also influences these decisions. Government policies promoting childbearing have shown mixed effectiveness, highlighting the need for their ongoing review and reform. Conclusion This review highlights the multifaceted determinants of childbearing intentions and underscores the importance of targeted interventions to address barriers and promote supportive family policies.

records.abstract: Delinquent taxpayers may find themselves on a government-imposed budget. The Internal Revenue Service tax collection rules that went into effect in September 1995 have had a dramatic impact on individual taxpayers who owe $10,000 or more in unpaid taxes. The new rules impose expense limits for housing, transportation and standard (food, housekeeping supplies, apparel, personal care products and services and miscellaneous items). Delinquent taxpayers have one year to adjust their lifestyles (slash expenses and sell assets) or face enforced collection action, such as wage levies and asset seizures, if they are unable to pay their taxes in full in three years or pay on installments using the IRS's mandated expense limits. Many taxpayers faced with spending limits will look to their CPAs for guidance on handling unpaid taxes. ENFORCED BUDGET Although the three-year rule cited above seems to permit taxpayers to avoid the IRS expense limits if they can pay the balance in full within three years, the practical effect of the new rules has been to place all delinquent taxpayers on a budget. The reason for this is that IRS field personnel use the expense limits as a starting point in computing what taxpayers can afford to pay. The IRS completes the revised Form 433-A, Collection Information Statement (section V of which--Monthly Income and Expense Analysis--is shown in exhibit 1, page 44) using national and local standards. The tax collection rules--contained in section 5323 of the Internal Revenue Manual--work as follows: 1. The IRS determines whether a taxpayer has assets that can be liquidated to pay the tax or some part of it. For example, a taxpayer can be asked to borrow against a home or cash in an individual retirement account. 2. If there are no readily available assets, the taxpayer's monthly gross income less necessary living expenses will be calculated to yield the minimum acceptable installment amount. Expenses are either necessary or conditional. Necessary expenses are those required for health and welfare or for the production of income, such as food, housing, taxes, health care and transportation. All other expenses are conditional, meaning they are not allowed if a taxpayer cannot pay in full in three years. Examples are private school or college tuition, repayment of student loans, voluntary contributions to retirement plans and credit card payments. National standard expenses are based on family size and income, as shown in exhibit 2, page 44. Housing expense limits are set on a county-by-county basis. Transportation expenses are set on a regional and metropolitan basis. PRACTICAL RULES FOR CPAs Internal Revenue Manual exhibit 5300 contains elaborate charts and lists of questions and answers concerning the new collection standards. Some practical rules for CPAs: 1. Do not let clients submit the financial information on their own to the IRS collection division. Practitioners should carefully go over a taxpayer's assets, liabilities, income and expenses, looking for items that will deviate from the guidelines. For example, a taxpayer with a special medical diet--properly documented--can receive a higher food allowance. A taxpayer with high unreimbursed employee expenses or who is making court-ordered payments (such as child support) should document them as well. 2. Some clients may be able to delay imposition of expense limits. A taxpayer with sufficient assets to fully pay the liability if penalties can be abated or--in the case of nonfilers--if the proper returns are filed and the amount due is adjusted, should be advised to ask for a delay to accomplish the abatement or file the returns. …

records.title: Financial Aid 101: Planning Opportunities for CPAs
records.venue: Journal of accountancy online/Journal of accountancy
records.abstract: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY * COLLEGES AWARD FINANCIAL AID IN THE FORM OF scholarships, grants, loans and work-study awards based on the financial need of a student. The formula used to determine financial need is: financial need = cost of attendance (COA) - expected family contribution (EFC). * THE EFC IS DEPENDENT ON THE INCOME AND ASSETS of parents and student and is determined by filing the free application for federal student aid (FAFSA) every year that a child will be in college. * Generally, any income and assets parents have in excess of $100,000 will significantly reduce their eligibility for financial aid for children in college. * The federal methodology is used by most institutions for awarding financial aid, but some private colleges and a select group of elite schools use other methodologies. * CPAs CAN PROVIDE A VALUABLE SERVICE TO THEIR clients by assisting in the filing of the FAFSA form and planning to maximize financial aid awards. With college costs increasing faster than the rate of inflation and the annual price tag at many private colleges now exceeding $40,000, financing a college education has become more daunting than ever. CPAs increasingly are being asked for advice on how to save for college and how to maximize financial aid awards. While it is tempting to recommend saving in a child's name because of the lower tax rate or investing in prepaid tuition plans to gain immunity from tuition hikes, such actions can dramatically reduce financial aid awards. Estimating financial needs and devising tax-effective investment strategies are important (see Other Considerations, page 83), but relying exclusively on tax-favored investments for college can negate the fruits of hard work and planning if the result is a reduced financial aid award. CPAs can play a key role in advising clients on investment and tax strategies to finance college education. In this article we'll analyze the federal financial aid formula, explain the effects of different factors on financial aid awards and offer planning opportunities CPAs can consider for their clients. THE FORMULA Colleges awarding scholarships, grants, loans and work-study programs based on the student's financial need use the following formula: Financial need = cost of attendance (COA) - expected family contribution (EFC). COA is the total yearly cost including tuition and fees, on-campus room and board (or a housing and food allowance for off-campus students), books, supplies, transportation, loan fees and miscellaneous expenses, including an allowance for the rental or purchase of a personal computer. The EFC is dependent on the income and assets of parents and student. Exhibit 1, page 81, diagrams the components of the EFC. The EFC is determined by filing the free application for federal student aid (FAFSA) every year that a child attends college. This is an additional service CPAs could provide their clients and is easily done at the time the client's tax return is prepared. The FAFSA should be filed after January 1 of each year; it can be filed electronically at www.fafsa. ed.gov. Computation of the EFC is a process akin to filling out an income tax return. To maximize financial aid awards, CPAs need a sound understanding of the rules. To illustrate how the financial aid formula works, let's assume the following facts for the Jones family for 2004: Family: Size (2 parents, 2 children) 4 Number of children attending college 1 State of residence Massachusetts Parents: Age of the older parent 50 Earned income of parent 1 $40,000 Earned income of parent 2 $20,000 Adjusted gross income $63,000 Contributions to 401(k) plans $6,000 Assessable assets $50,000 Student: Earned income $4,000 Adjusted gross income $4,200 Assessable assets $5,000 The calculations of the EFC for the Jones family are presented in exhibit 2, page 82, and explained below. …
